Tretinoin.summary: Prescription topical retinoid with extensive documentation for photoaging and acne; used to smooth fine wrinkles and reduce acne.
Tretinoin.overview:
Tretinoin is all-trans retinoic acid, the biologically active form of vitamin A, and is sold as a prescription topical cream, gel or lotion under brands such as Retin-A. It was first developed for acne and later became the best-documented topical treatment for photoaged skin, where it is used to soften fine lines, even out pigmentation and improve texture.

In appearance-focused communities it is widely described as the benchmark anti-aging and acne ingredient. Clinical evidence includes long-term vehicle-controlled trials and systematic reviews, although many trials are small and use differing formulations and outcome measures.
Tretinoin.mechanism: Tretinoin binds nuclear retinoic acid receptors (RARs) and retinoid X receptors in skin cells and changes gene expression. This speeds up keratinocyte turnover, normalizes follicular keratinization so pores clog less, and reduces inflammation. In dermal fibroblasts it increases collagen synthesis and reduces the activity of matrix metalloproteinases that break collagen down, which underlies the improvements seen in photodamage. Because it is already the active acid, it does not need conversion in the skin, unlike retinol.
Tretinoin.risks: Irritation (redness, dryness, peeling, stinging) is common, particularly in the first weeks, and increased sun sensitivity is reported, so daily sun protection is advised. Topical retinoids are generally avoided in pregnancy because of the known teratogenic risk of systemic retinoids, even though systemic absorption from topical use is low. It is prescription-only in most countries. Results build slowly over months and fade if use stops.

Retinol.summary: Over-the-counter vitamin A derivative that converts to retinoic acid in skin.
Retinol.note: Reported to be weaker than tretinoin; sold without a prescription.
Retinol.overview:
Retinol is a form of vitamin A (an alcohol) used in over-the-counter serums and creams for fine lines, uneven tone and rough texture. It is one of the most common anti-aging cosmetic ingredients and is often positioned as a gentler step toward prescription retinoids.

Evidence for improvement in photoaged skin exists in clinical studies and reviews, but results are generally slower and milder than with tretinoin, and product concentration, formulation stability and packaging heavily influence real-world performance.
Retinol.mechanism: After it enters the skin, retinol is oxidized in two enzymatic steps to retinaldehyde and then to retinoic acid, which activates retinoic acid receptors and alters gene expression. The downstream effects are increased epidermal turnover, greater collagen production and less breakdown of existing collagen. Because conversion is limited and inefficient, the amount of retinoic acid generated is small, which explains both its milder effect and its better tolerability.
Retinol.risks: Dryness, redness, flaking and photosensitivity are the usual side effects and tend to ease with gradual introduction and moisturizer. Retinol is oxidation- and light-sensitive, so poorly formulated products may lose potency. Dermatology guidance generally advises avoiding topical retinoids during pregnancy as a precaution. It is sold without prescription but concentrations are regulated in some regions.

Adapalene.summary: Topical retinoid for acne and texture, sold over the counter in the US since 2016.
Adapalene.overview:
Adapalene is a synthetic third-generation topical retinoid developed for acne vulgaris. It became the first retinoid sold over the counter for acne in the United States in 2016 (as a 0.1% gel), following earlier prescription availability, and is also marketed in combination with benzoyl peroxide or clindamycin.

Beyond acne it is used off-label for texture, keratosis pilaris and some signs of photoaging. Many users describe it as the most accessible retinoid, since it can be bought without a prescription and is reported to cause less irritation than tretinoin.
Adapalene.mechanism: Adapalene selectively activates retinoic acid receptors beta and gamma, which normalizes follicular keratinocyte differentiation, prevents microcomedone formation and has direct anti-inflammatory effects. It is chemically more stable than tretinoin and less affected by light and benzoyl peroxide, which makes it easy to combine with other acne actives.
Adapalene.risks: Initial dryness, redness, burning and peeling are common and typically peak in the first few weeks. Photosensitivity is reported, and daily sunscreen is generally advised. Use in pregnancy is generally discouraged despite reassuring limited human data. Benefits take about 8 to 12 weeks to appear, and combining with other irritants can worsen tolerability.

Tazarotene.summary: Prescription topical retinoid approved for acne, psoriasis and photodamage; generally considered among the most potent.
Tazarotene.overview:
Tazarotene is a prescription acetylenic topical retinoid approved for acne vulgaris, plaque psoriasis and, in cream form, for facial fine wrinkling and pigment irregularities from sun damage. It is generally considered one of the most potent topical retinoids.

Its potency leads to its use in stubborn acne and photodamage, but irritation is a frequent limiting factor, so newer lotion and foam formulations and combinations with other agents have been developed.
Tazarotene.mechanism: Tazarotene is a prodrug converted in the skin to tazarotenic acid, which selectively binds retinoic acid receptors beta and gamma. This normalizes keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, reduces inflammation and influences genes involved in skin repair, producing improvements in acne lesions, psoriatic plaques and photoaged skin.
Tazarotene.risks: Local irritation, dryness, peeling and photosensitivity are common. Tazarotene carries a boxed pregnancy warning in some labels because of teratogenicity concerns, and pregnancy testing and contraception are advised for people who could become pregnant. It requires a prescription.

Isotretinoin.summary: Oral retinoid reserved for severe, scarring or treatment-resistant acne, used under strict medical supervision.
Isotretinoin.overview:
Isotretinoin (13-cis retinoic acid, formerly sold as Accutane) is an oral retinoid reserved for severe, scarring or treatment-resistant acne. It is described as the only acne therapy capable of producing long-lasting remission in many patients and is also used off-label for severe rosacea and some other conditions.

In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a treatment for severe acne, and its side-effect burden and regulatory controls mean it is used under medical supervision.
Isotretinoin.mechanism: Isotretinoin markedly reduces the size of sebaceous glands and lowers sebum output, normalizes follicular keratinization, reduces growth of acne-associated bacteria indirectly by changing the follicular environment, and has anti-inflammatory effects. It likely acts partly through induction of cell death in sebocytes and changes in retinoid-responsive gene expression.
Isotretinoin.risks: It is a potent teratogen and is distributed under strict risk-management programs (such as iPLEDGE in the US) requiring pregnancy prevention. Common effects include dry lips, skin and eyes; laboratory monitoring is needed for lipids and liver enzymes. Reports of mood changes have been studied extensively, and a recent meta-analysis found no clear increase in suicide risk, though monitoring remains standard. It is prescription-only.

Botulinum toxin A.summary: Purified neurotoxin injected to relax targeted facial muscles and soften dynamic wrinkles.
Botulinum toxin A.overview:
Botulinum toxin type A is a purified neurotoxin injected in tiny amounts to weaken targeted muscles. Products such as onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) are among the most common cosmetic procedures worldwide and are used to soften dynamic wrinkles such as frown lines, forehead lines and crow's feet.

Beyond wrinkle treatment, practitioners use it for masseter slimming, brow shaping and other contouring effects. It is also approved for numerous medical indications, including migraine and spasticity. Results are temporary and require repeat treatment.
Botulinum toxin A.mechanism: The toxin enters motor nerve terminals and cleaves SNAP-25, a protein in the SNARE complex needed to release acetylcholine. Without acetylcholine release the injected muscle relaxes, and overlying skin creases soften because the muscle can no longer fold it. Effects last a few months until nerve terminals regenerate.
Botulinum toxin A.risks: Typical effects are bruising, headache and temporary asymmetry or drooping of an eyelid or brow if the toxin spreads to unintended muscles. Rare systemic spread can cause serious weakness. Some patients develop reduced response over time, possibly linked to neutralizing antibodies. It is a prescription drug that is administered by trained clinicians; counterfeit products are a recognized hazard.

Azelaic acid.summary: Topical dicarboxylic acid used for acne, rosacea and hyperpigmentation.
Azelaic acid.overview:
Azelaic acid is a naturally occurring dicarboxylic acid used topically for acne, rosacea and post-inflammatory or melasma-type hyperpigmentation. Prescription strengths of 15 to 20 percent exist, and lower-strength cosmetic versions are sold over the counter in many markets.

It is used for its breadth of action: a single ingredient addresses bumps, redness and dark marks, and it is generally acceptable in people who cannot tolerate retinoids.
Azelaic acid.mechanism: Azelaic acid has antibacterial effects against acne-associated bacteria, normalizes follicular keratinization, suppresses inflammatory pathways and reactive oxygen species, and competitively inhibits tyrosinase in overactive melanocytes, which explains its use in hyperpigmentation.
Azelaic acid.risks: Stinging, itching and dryness are the most common effects and usually fade with continued use. Systemic absorption is low and it is widely considered compatible with pregnancy, though individual advice should come from a clinician. Results take weeks to months.

Niacinamide.summary: Vitamin B3 form used in cosmetics for barrier support, oil control and more even pigment.
Niacinamide.overview:
Niacinamide (nicotinamide) is the amide form of vitamin B3 and a staple ingredient in cosmetic serums and moisturizers. Typical claims include improved barrier function, reduced oil appearance and pore prominence, calmer redness and a more even tone.

Clinical studies support modest benefits for hyperpigmentation, barrier function and some inflammatory acne, but effect sizes are generally small and vary between formulations.
Niacinamide.mechanism: Niacinamide is a precursor of NAD+ and NADP+, coenzymes central to cellular energy and repair. In skin it increases ceramide and barrier lipid synthesis, reduces sebum output and interferes with the transfer of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes, helping to lighten uneven pigment.
Niacinamide.risks: It is generally very well tolerated. Occasional flushing, itching or irritation occurs, especially at higher concentrations or in poorly formulated products. It is sold freely as a cosmetic ingredient.

Vitamin C (topical).summary: Topical antioxidant used to brighten skin, fade dark spots and support collagen synthesis.
Vitamin C (topical).overview:
Topical vitamin C, most often as L-ascorbic acid, is used in serums intended to brighten the complexion, fade dark spots and provide antioxidant protection against environmental damage. It is among the best-known cosmeceuticals, popular alongside sunscreen in morning routines.

Studies suggest benefits for photoaging and hyperpigmentation, but trials are often small, sometimes industry-funded, and effectiveness is highly dependent on formulation, pH, concentration and stability.
Vitamin C (topical).mechanism: Ascorbic acid neutralizes free radicals generated by ultraviolet exposure, is a required cofactor for enzymes that stabilize collagen, and inhibits tyrosinase to reduce melanin production. It also helps regenerate vitamin E in skin. Skin penetration requires an acidic, adequately concentrated formulation.
Vitamin C (topical).risks: L-ascorbic acid oxidizes easily, turning serums yellow or brown and reducing potency. Stinging and irritation can occur, particularly with low-pH products. It is not regarded as a substitute for sunscreen and is sold over the counter.

Tranexamic acid.summary: Antifibrinolytic drug used in dermatology for melasma and hyperpigmentation, topically or orally (oral requires a prescription).
Tranexamic acid.overview:
Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic drug first used to control bleeding. In dermatology it has become a popular option for melasma and stubborn hyperpigmentation, applied topically, injected in clinics or taken by mouth.

The cosmetic use of oral tranexamic acid is off-label and prescription-only, while topical products are sold over the counter in many places. Studies show meaningful improvement in melasma but with heterogeneous designs and recurrence after stopping.
Tranexamic acid.mechanism: It blocks plasmin formation, and in skin this appears to reduce plasmin-driven stimulation of melanocytes and related inflammatory and vascular signalling, decreasing melanin production and the vascular component of melasma.
Tranexamic acid.risks: Topical use is usually well tolerated, with mild irritation. Oral tranexamic acid carries a risk of blood clots and is unsuitable for people with a history of thromboembolism or those on estrogen-containing contraception; gastrointestinal upset and menstrual changes are possible. Oral use requires medical screening and supervision.

Hydroquinone.summary: Topical skin-lightening agent for melasma and dark spots, long regarded as the reference standard among depigmenting treatments.
Hydroquinone.overview:
Hydroquinone is a long-established skin-lightening agent used for melasma, sun spots and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. It has been regarded as the reference standard among topical depigmenting treatments, typically as a prescription product or compounded formulation.

Regulation differs by country, with some regions restricting or banning cosmetic use and others permitting it under prescription control.
Hydroquinone.mechanism: Hydroquinone inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin synthesis, and also impairs melanosome formation and promotes melanocyte degradation, resulting in reduced pigment production.
Hydroquinone.risks: Common effects are irritation and contact dermatitis. Prolonged or high-concentration use, especially of unregulated products, can cause exogenous ochronosis, a hard-to-treat blue-black discoloration, and paradoxical darkening. Continuous use is usually limited to short courses under supervision. Safety questions about systemic exposure have led to restrictions in several jurisdictions.

Alpha-arbutin.summary: Hydroquinone-derived tyrosinase inhibitor in over-the-counter serums for dark spots, marketed as gentler than hydroquinone.
Alpha-arbutin.overview:
Alpha-arbutin is a synthetic glucoside of hydroquinone used in over-the-counter serums to fade dark spots and even skin tone. It is marketed as a gentler alternative to hydroquinone. The Grokipedia page covers arbutin generally, including the alpha form.

Evidence is limited: laboratory and small clinical studies support lightening activity, but high-quality controlled trials in humans are sparse.
Alpha-arbutin.mechanism: Alpha-arbutin competitively inhibits tyrosinase and slows melanin synthesis. Unlike hydroquinone, it is released slowly in the skin, which is thought to produce a milder effect with lower toxicity to melanocytes.
Alpha-arbutin.risks: Side effects are generally mild, including occasional irritation. Because it can release small amounts of hydroquinone, regulators set concentration limits for cosmetic use in some regions, and reported effectiveness is modest compared with prescription treatments.

Kojic acid.summary: Fungal-derived tyrosinase inhibitor used in skin-brightening products.
Kojic acid.overview:
Kojic acid is a compound produced by Aspergillus fungi during fermentation of foods such as rice, and it is used in lightening soaps, creams and serums for dark spots and melasma.

Dermatology studies have compared it with other agents for melasma, with some reporting favorable results, but evidence is moderate in quality and often relies on small trials.
Kojic acid.mechanism: Kojic acid chelates copper at the active site of tyrosinase, inhibiting the enzyme that begins melanin synthesis. It also has antioxidant activity.
Kojic acid.risks: Contact dermatitis and irritation are the primary concerns, and some regions limit cosmetic concentrations. It is unstable in light and air. Long-term safety data are limited and it is not a substitute for sun protection.

Cysteamine.summary: Topical depigmenting agent; controlled melasma studies report improvement over vehicle.
Cysteamine.overview:
Cysteamine is an aminothiol drug approved for treating nephropathic cystinosis, and a topical cream is also used for melasma and hyperpigmentation. Its dermatologic use is positioned as a non-hydroquinone depigmenting option.

Controlled studies in melasma have shown improvement compared with vehicle, though trials are modest in size.
Cysteamine.mechanism: In skin, cysteamine is thought to inhibit tyrosinase and peroxidase, scavenge free radicals and chelate iron and copper, reducing melanin formation.
Cysteamine.risks: The main reported drawbacks are a strong sulfurous odor, stinging and redness, and the instability of the molecule in water. Systemic cysteamine drugs have additional gastrointestinal and other side effects, and its availability as a cosmetic versus a medicine varies by country.

Salicylic acid.summary: Oil-soluble beta hydroxy acid that penetrates pores; used for acne and blackheads.
Salicylic acid.overview:
Salicylic acid is a beta hydroxy acid derived from willow bark chemistry and used in washes, toners and spot treatments for acne, blackheads and oily skin, as well as in treatments for warts, dandruff and keratosis pilaris.

Its oil solubility lets it work inside pores, which makes it a standard over-the-counter acne ingredient at concentrations up to a few percent.
Salicylic acid.mechanism: Salicylic acid is a keratolytic that loosens the bonds between corneocytes and dissolves intercellular lipids in clogged follicles, helping clear comedones. It also has mild anti-inflammatory effects.
Salicylic acid.risks: Dryness, peeling and irritation are common. Large-area or high-strength use can cause salicylate absorption and toxicity, so caution is advised in children, in pregnancy and over broken skin. Photosensitivity is mild, and sunscreen use is advised.

Glycolic acid.summary: Alpha hydroxy acid exfoliant used for dullness, rough texture and surface renewal.
Glycolic acid.overview:
Glycolic acid is the smallest alpha hydroxy acid and one of the most widely used chemical exfoliants. Lower-strength products are used at home for dullness and rough texture, and higher concentrations are applied in professional peels.

Studies show improvements in photoaged skin texture and fine lines with regular use, although stronger peels carry greater risk.
Glycolic acid.mechanism: By weakening the bonds between surface skin cells, glycolic acid promotes exfoliation, and with repeated use it stimulates epidermal renewal and has been reported to increase dermal collagen and glycosaminoglycans.
Glycolic acid.risks: Stinging, redness and peeling are frequent, and the skin becomes more sensitive to ultraviolet light, so sunscreen use is advised. Excess strength or poor technique can cause burns and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, especially in darker skin tones.

Lactic acid.summary: Alpha hydroxy acid that exfoliates and acts as a humectant; typically milder than glycolic acid.
Lactic acid.overview:
Lactic acid is an alpha hydroxy acid used in exfoliating serums, peels and body lotions. It is often chosen by people with sensitive skin because it is typically milder than glycolic acid.

It has been studied for hyperpigmentation and photoaged skin, and it also contributes to natural moisturizing factor in the skin.
Lactic acid.mechanism: Lactic acid loosens connections between dead skin cells to promote exfoliation, and it also acts as a humectant that supports hydration. Larger molecular size than glycolic acid limits penetration depth.
Lactic acid.risks: Irritation, stinging and increased sun sensitivity occur, and professional-strength peels carry a risk of pigment changes. Sunscreen is advised.

Ceramides.summary: Skin-barrier lipids used in moisturizers to reduce dryness and water loss.
Ceramides.overview:
Ceramides are waxy lipids that make up roughly half of the lipid matrix of the outer skin layer. Moisturizers containing ceramides, often with cholesterol and fatty acids, are used to repair barrier damage, ease dryness and support skin affected by eczema or retinoid irritation.

Clinical trials generally show improved barrier function and hydration compared with simple emollients, though the advantage over other well-made moisturizers can be modest.
Ceramides.mechanism: Topical ceramides help replenish the intercellular lipid lamellae in the stratum corneum, which reduces transepidermal water loss and restores the barrier against irritants and allergens.
Ceramides.risks: They are among the best-tolerated skincare ingredients, with rare allergic reactions to other formulation components. They are over the counter and benefits depend heavily on the full formula.

Urea.summary: Humectant and keratolytic used for rough, dry, scaling skin.
Urea.overview:
Urea is a natural component of skin moisturizing factor and is used in creams for dry, rough or scaling skin, including xerosis, eczema, keratosis pilaris and calloused heels. Low concentrations hydrate, while higher concentrations soften thick scale.

It has a long record in dermatology and clinical support as a moisturizer and keratolytic.
Urea.mechanism: Urea attracts and binds water as a humectant and, at higher concentrations, breaks down hydrogen bonds in keratin to loosen and shed dead skin. It also appears to improve barrier function and antimicrobial peptide expression.
Urea.risks: Mild stinging is the main side effect, especially on cracked or inflamed skin and at higher strengths. It is available without a prescription in most markets.

Hyaluronic acid.summary: Glycosaminoglycan used topically for hydration and, in cross-linked form, as an injectable dermal filler.
Hyaluronic acid.overview:
Hyaluronic acid is a glycosaminoglycan found in skin and joints, used in topical serums for hydration and in cross-linked injectable gels as dermal fillers. Topical products temporarily plump and hydrate the surface, while fillers add structural volume to lips, cheeks and folds.

Claims that it holds roughly a thousand times its weight in water refer to laboratory behavior; in practice topical benefits are mostly short-term hydration, whereas injectables have stronger clinical evidence for volume restoration.
Hyaluronic acid.mechanism: As a humectant polymer, it binds large amounts of water in the skin surface or in injected gel. Cross-linked fillers physically add volume and may stimulate modest collagen production through tissue stretch.
Hyaluronic acid.risks: Topical forms are very well tolerated. Injectable fillers can cause bruising, swelling and lumps, and rare vascular occlusion leading to tissue necrosis or vision loss, and outcomes are associated with injector skill. Fillers are medical devices administered by trained injectors.

GHK-Cu.summary: Copper-binding peptide studied for collagen remodeling, wound repair and follicle biology; human evidence is limited to small topical studies.
GHK-Cu.note: The FDA has flagged injectable versions as a significant safety risk.
GHK-Cu.overview:
GHK-Cu is a naturally occurring copper-binding tripeptide (glycyl-histidyl-lysine) found in plasma and other fluids, with levels declining with age. It is used in anti-aging creams and sold as a research peptide with claims about skin, wound repair and hair.

Human evidence is mostly limited to small topical studies, with most other findings coming from laboratory and animal work.
GHK-Cu.mechanism: GHK-Cu is proposed to act as a signalling molecule that stimulates collagen and glycosaminoglycan production, modulates metalloproteinases and influences many genes tied to tissue remodeling and inflammation. These mechanisms are largely demonstrated in cells and animals.
GHK-Cu.risks: Topical cosmetic use is usually well tolerated apart from occasional irritation. Injectable and compounded versions are not approved, and the FDA has flagged safety concerns about them, including immunogenicity and impurity risks. Research-use peptides sold online have variable quality.

Matrixyl.summary: Cosmetic signaling peptide marketed for collagen and fine lines; supporting data are mainly supplier-sponsored or small studies.
Matrixyl.overview:
Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, Pal-KTTKS) is a lipid-modified fragment of type I procollagen developed by a cosmetic ingredient supplier for anti-wrinkle products. It appears in many serums and eye creams.

Supporting data are mainly from supplier-sponsored or small studies, so independent evidence of visible improvement is limited.
Matrixyl.mechanism: The peptide is thought to mimic collagen breakdown fragments that signal fibroblasts to make new collagen and other matrix components. The palmitoyl group is added to help it cross the skin barrier.
Matrixyl.risks: It is considered low-risk, with rare irritation, and is freely sold as a cosmetic. Effects are modest and benefits depend on formulation and the concentration achieved at the target layer.

Argireline.summary: Peptide marketed as a topical alternative to botulinum toxin; supporting studies are small and often manufacturer-linked.
Argireline.overview:
Argireline (acetyl hexapeptide-8, formerly acetyl hexapeptide-3) is a short synthetic peptide marketed as a topical alternative to botulinum toxin for expression lines, particularly around the eyes and forehead.

Most supportive studies are small, short and often manufacturer-linked, and any reported effect is far milder than injected toxin.
Argireline.mechanism: It mimics the N-terminal end of SNAP-25 and is proposed to compete with it in the SNARE complex, slightly reducing acetylcholine release and muscle contraction. Whether enough peptide penetrates the skin to do this in practice is questioned.
Argireline.risks: It is generally well tolerated and sold as a cosmetic. Skin penetration is reported to be poor, and real-world benefit is uncertain.

SNAP-8.summary: Cosmetic peptide in the same family as Argireline, marketed for expression lines; independent evidence is scarce.
SNAP-8.overview:
SNAP-8 (acetyl octapeptide-3) is a longer analogue of Argireline marketed for reducing expression wrinkles. It appears in anti-aging serums and eye creams.

Publicly available evidence is limited and mostly from manufacturers; independent controlled trials are scarce.
SNAP-8.mechanism: Like Argireline, it is designed to imitate part of SNAP-25 and interfere with SNARE complex assembly to lower neurotransmitter release at the muscle junction, though skin delivery is reported to limit its effect.
SNAP-8.risks: It is considered low risk and is unrestricted as a cosmetic ingredient. Reported effects are modest and reversible.

Carnosine.summary: Dipeptide with antioxidant and anti-glycation properties, studied for skin aging.
Carnosine.overview:
Carnosine is a dipeptide of beta-alanine and histidine found in muscle and brain, and it appears in some skincare products and supplements positioned for antioxidant and anti-glycation benefits.

Skin-related data are preliminary, mostly from lab studies and small trials, while its best human evidence is as a source of beta-alanine for muscle buffering.
Carnosine.mechanism: Carnosine scavenges reactive oxygen species, chelates metal ions and inhibits glycation, the process of sugars cross-linking proteins like collagen. These effects are demonstrated mainly in vitro.
Carnosine.risks: It is generally well tolerated; beta-alanine supplementation can cause tingling. Evidence for visible skin improvement is limited.

Spironolactone.summary: Prescription antiandrogen and diuretic used off-label for hormonal acne in adult women.
Spironolactone.overview:
Spironolactone is a prescription diuretic and aldosterone antagonist that also blocks androgen receptors. Dermatologists use it off-label for persistent hormonal acne in adult women and sometimes for female pattern hair loss and hirsutism.

Observational studies and small trials support benefit for adult female acne, though large randomized evidence has been limited until recent years.
Spironolactone.mechanism: By antagonizing androgen receptors and reducing androgen production, it reduces sebum output and the androgen-driven stimulation of sebaceous glands.
Spironolactone.risks: Side effects include menstrual irregularity, breast tenderness, dizziness and raised potassium. It is not suitable in pregnancy because of feminization risk to a male fetus, and is generally not used for acne in men because of feminizing effects. It requires a prescription and monitoring.

Clascoterone.summary: Topical antiandrogen approved by the FDA for acne in 2020; being studied for hair loss.
Clascoterone.overview:
Clascoterone (Winlevi) is a topical antiandrogen cream approved by the FDA in 2020 for acne in patients aged 12 and older, notable as the first new acne drug class in decades. A solution is being investigated for androgenetic alopecia.

Phase 3 trials showed greater lesion reduction than vehicle, and real-world case series report similar results.
Clascoterone.mechanism: It competes with dihydrotestosterone for androgen receptors in sebaceous glands and hair follicles, blocking local androgen signalling without much systemic effect.
Clascoterone.risks: Local redness, dryness and itching are most common. Rare, reversible suppression of the adrenal axis was seen under maximal-use conditions, so caution is advised in young patients. It is prescription-only, and its hair-loss use remains investigational.

PDRN / Polynucleotides.summary: Salmon-derived DNA fragments used in injectable and topical "skin booster" treatments; results vary by formulation.
PDRN / Polynucleotides.overview:
PDRN (polydeoxyribonucleotide) is a mixture of DNA fragments, typically extracted from salmon or trout sperm, used in injectable and topical 'skin booster' treatments marketed for rejuvenation, scar improvement and wound healing. It is popular in Korean aesthetic clinics.

Evidence comes from small clinical studies and wound-healing research, and formulations, sources and molecular sizes vary widely, so results are not reliably comparable.
PDRN / Polynucleotides.mechanism: PDRN is proposed to act through adenosine A2A receptor activation and by providing nucleotides for the salvage pathway, supporting fibroblast activity, angiogenesis and reduced inflammation.
PDRN / Polynucleotides.risks: Injection carries risks of bruising, infection and allergy, particularly to fish-derived material. Regulatory status varies and many cosmetic products are not approved as drugs. Independent evidence for lasting aesthetic benefit remains limited.

Omega-3 (EPA/DHA).summary: Anti-inflammatory fatty acids discussed in relation to skin, recovery and general health; skin results are mixed.
Omega-3 (EPA/DHA).overview:
Omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA come from oily fish, fish oil and algae and are taken for cardiovascular and general health. In appearance contexts they are discussed for skin inflammation, dryness, UV tolerance and recovery.

Results for skin are mixed and modest; the strongest evidence for EPA and DHA concerns triglyceride lowering rather than cosmetic outcomes.
Omega-3 (EPA/DHA).mechanism: EPA and DHA are incorporated into cell membranes and serve as precursors to specialized pro-resolving mediators such as resolvins and protectins, which help turn off inflammation.
Omega-3 (EPA/DHA).risks: Fish oil can cause fishy aftertaste and digestive upset, and high doses may raise bleeding risk or affect heart rhythm in some people. Contaminant and oxidation quality vary by product. Supplements are sold over the counter.

Zinc.summary: Essential mineral used for inflammatory acne and deficiency-related hair shedding; benefit is best supported when deficiency is corrected.
Zinc.note: Evidence of benefit is strongest in people who were deficient.
Zinc.overview:
Zinc is an essential mineral used as an oral supplement and in topical products, including zinc oxide sunscreens and acne formulations. People use it for inflammatory acne and for hair shedding associated with deficiency.

Benefits are most convincing when actual deficiency is corrected; in zinc-replete people, evidence for improved acne or appearance is limited.
Zinc.mechanism: Zinc supports enzyme function, wound healing, immune regulation and keratinocyte biology, and it has mild anti-inflammatory and antibacterial effects that are thought to relate to acne improvement.
Zinc.risks: High-dose supplementation can cause nausea and, over time, copper deficiency. Intake above requirements has not been shown to offer additional benefit. Zinc is available without prescription.
